Florida Seizes 163 Illegal Slot Machines in Raid

Published September 16, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Florida's Gaming Control Commission, working with local and state law enforcement, dismantled two unlicensed gambling operations in St. Petersburg on September 16 in a sting the agency named "Operation Final Spin," seizing 163 gambling machines and nearly $250,000 in cash.

What was seized, and where

Investigators removed 90 machines and $142,020 in cash from a business called Action Arcade, and 73 machines and $105,265 in cash from a second location, The Zoo Sports Club and Grille — a combined 163 devices and roughly $247,000. The operation involved the Florida Gaming Control Commission alongside the Pinellas County Sheriff's Office, the Florida Highway Patrol, and the Department of Business and Professional Regulation's Division of Alcoholic Beverages and Tobacco.

Charges and the agency's broader campaign

Three individuals connected to the two businesses were issued notices to appear in court, facing charges that include possession of slot machines and operating or working at an illegal gambling house. Florida state representative Berny Jacques, commenting on the raid, said the machines "are designed to take advantage of people, and far too often that means senior citizens living on fixed incomes." The FGCC noted this operation adds to more than 200 illegal arcades the agency has shut down previously, while also acknowledging that enforcement alone hasn't been enough to eliminate the underlying problem.

Why it matters to US casino players

Unlicensed slot parlors operating outside a state's regulatory framework offer players none of the consumer protections that come with a licensed casino floor or regulated online casino platform — no certified payout testing, no responsible-gambling tools, and no real recourse if a machine simply doesn't pay as advertised. Florida's continued crackdown is part of a broader nationwide pattern of state regulators targeting unlicensed gaming machines and sweepstakes-style operations, and it's a useful reminder that a machine's legality in a given state isn't always obvious from the outside — sticking to licensed, regulated venues and platforms remains the more reliable way to know the games are actually tested and fair.
